full_text:

Investing.com-- Asian stock markets fell broadly on Tuesday as surging bond yields and higher oil prices pressured risk appetite, while investors awaited the Reserve Bank of Australia's interest-rate decision later in the day, with markets expecting another increase.
Regional stocks also took cues from their U.S. peers. Wall Street futures also traded lower in Asian trading after all three major indices fell modestly overnight.

Asia stocks weighed down by surging yields, oil prices
Japan's Nikkei 225 slipped 1.3% by 03:37 GMT, while the broader TOPIX index slid 1.5%.
South Korea's KOSPI fell 0.8%, while China's blue-chip CSI 300 and Shanghai Composite edged down 0.2% each.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index also declined 0.8%.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield climbed above 5.27% overnight, its highest level in 19 years. The two-year yield approached 5% as traders increased bets on further Federal Reserve rate increases through the middle of next year.
Higher yields raise the discount rate applied to equities and increase borrowing costs for governments and companies, putting pressure on high-growth technology stocks in particular.
Oil prices added to the inflation concerns. Brent crude rose to around $107 a barrel as there was no clear breakthrough in efforts to ease the conflict involving the United States and Iran and restore normal traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Tech stocks under pressure amid AI risks
Technology shares remained under pressure as signs of a slower pace of artificial intelligence development added to concerns about the huge investment underpinning the sector.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng TECH sub-index fell 1.2% on Tuesday, while Japan's top tech investor SoftBank Group (TYO:9984) slid 2%.
OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, its next-generation artificial intelligence model, after it failed internal safety controls, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.
The report followed news that OpenAI had paused training, evaluation and inference with tool use for some of its most capable models as it strengthens safety controls.
Investors were also digesting Anthropic's IPO prospectus, which offered a stark picture of both the scale and cost of the AI boom.
A Reuters report showed that the Claude maker's revenue rose nearly 12-fold to about $4.6 billion in 2025, but reported a $42 billion net loss, including a $34 billion accounting charge, while planning another $518 billion in cloud and infrastructure spending.
The prospectus also warned that increasingly capable AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks.
Chinese technology stocks remained particularly fragile after shares were hit on Monday by reports of U.S. plans to restrict Chinese components used in data centres.
RBA rate decision ahead, hike expected
In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 edged up 0.1% as investors remained focused on the RBA decision.
The RBA is widely expected to raise its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60%, which would be its highest level in nearly 15 years. Investors are likely to focus on Governor Michele Bullock's guidance on whether further tightening will be needed as higher oil prices add to inflation risks.
Elsewhere in Asia, Singapore's Straits Times Index dipped 0.3%. Futures tied to India's Nifty 50 ticked down 0.1%.
Investors also looked ahead to a busy U.S. data calendar, including inflation, manufacturing and labour-market reports, for clues on the path of Federal Reserve policy.

title: Anthropic prospectus shows $2 trln IPO ambition despite huge loss, Reuters reports
full_text:
U.S. stocks end down as OpenAI training halt weighs on AI trade, bonds extend rout
Investing.com-- Anthropic is heading toward a public debut that could test investors’ appetite for the enormous spending and valuations underpinning the artificial intelligence boom, Reuters reported on Monday, citing the company’s IPO prospectus.
The AI startup expects a valuation of more than $2 trillion, more than double its estimated $965 billion value in May, the report said.
Revenue surged 12-fold in 2025 to nearly $4.6 billion, but Anthropic reported a $42 billion net loss, including a roughly $34 billion accounting charge tied to financing instruments that could convert into shares, Reuters reported.
The company spent $7.33 billion on computing and infrastructure last year, three times its 2024 outlay, while forecasting $518 billion in cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations over the coming year, the report stated.
Anthropic’s operating loss exceeded $8 billion, excluding certain liability writedowns, highlighting the cost of scaling its Claude models. The company also warned that nearly a quarter of revenue came from two customers and that major clients could reduce spending.
The IPO, expected after the November U.S. midterm elections, would put Anthropic alongside OpenAI and other AI giants in the public markets and provide a valuation benchmark for the sector, Reuters reported.

title: Oil extends gains as U.S.-Iran stalemate overshadows Saudi flows
full_text:
U.S. stocks end down as OpenAI training halt weighs on AI trade, bonds extend rout
Investing.com-- Oil prices rose on Tuesday, extending gains from the previous session, as a lack of progress in U.S.-Iran diplomacy kept concerns over Middle East supply disruptions in focus despite a recovery in crude exports from the region.
As of 21:23 ET (01:23 GMT), Brent Oil Futures expiring in November rose 1.3% to $106.60 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures gained 1.1% to $93.60 per barrel.
Brent futures had climbed near $109 per barrel in the previous session but pared gains to settle around $105 a barrel.

Qatari mediators were expected to hold separate talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and U.S. officials, with discussions focused on an amended seven-day proposal put forward by Iran last week, Reuters reported on Monday, citing sources.
The sides remained pessimistic about reaching an agreement before the U.S. midterm elections, the report said.
The diplomatic uncertainty has offset evidence that physical oil flows are recovering.
Crude exports from key Middle Eastern producers rose to 12.8 million barrels per day in September, their highest level since February, according to preliminary Kpler data.
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates accounted for much of the increase. Saudi crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz were on track to rise sharply this month after Riyadh diverted shipments from the Red Sea port of Yanbu following damage to its East-West pipeline.
Saudi Arabia has now repaired the pipeline and resumed exports from Yanbu, restoring a key route that bypasses Hormuz. The pipeline can transport up to 7 million barrels per day, while about 3.5 million bpd was flowing through it after the restart, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Higher exports have not fully eased the market's concerns because transporting crude around the Gulf remains costly and difficult.
The disruption has also tightened refined-product markets. Record diesel prices have prompted the White House to consider regulatory changes that could broaden sales of red-dyed diesel, Reuters reported, while speculation over possible U.S. diesel export restrictions has widened the Brent-WTI spread.

title: Gold steadies near seven-week low after 4% plunge as Fed hike bets rise
full_text:
U.S. stocks end down as OpenAI training halt weighs on AI trade, bonds extend rout
Investing.com -- Gold prices steadied near a seven-week low on Tuesday after tumbling 4% in the previous session, as the standoff between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz kept energy prices elevated and reinforced expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
At 21:11 ET (01:11 GMT), XAU/USD was little changed at $4,118.54 an ounce, while Gold Futures fell 0.4% to $4,150.26. XAG/USD rose 0.1% to $60.70, while XPT/USD slipped 0.3% to $1,711.94. The U.S. Dollar Index was little changed at 101.2.
Hormuz impasse keeps oil, Treasury yields elevated
Oil prices extended gains as Iran remained firm on its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian officials had privately expressed pessimism about reaching an agreement with Washington to end hostilities before the U.S. midterm elections in November, after President Donald Trump rejected Tehran's latest proposal to reopen the critical waterway within seven days.
The U.S.-Iran conflict is now in its eighth month, keeping pressure on global energy flows and inflation expectations.
The renewed rise in oil prices also intensified the selloff in the U.S. Treasury market on Monday. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to a fresh 19-year high, increasing the cost of holding gold, which does not generate interest income.
The Treasury selloff that began after the U.S.-Iran conflict erupted in late February has accelerated over the past month, raising fresh risks for the economy as higher yields push up borrowing costs.
The Trump administration has sought to ease pressure on longer-dated borrowing costs by increasing Treasury buybacks, but yields have continued to rise.
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said the increase in long-term yields reflects several factors, including a stronger growth outlook, concerns about government debt and expectations for additional interest rate increases.
Gold falls 7% in September as Fed outlook tightens
Gold has now fallen about 7% in September, despite reaching around $4,510 earlier this month. The decline follows the Fed's first interest rate increase since 2023, with policymakers also leaving open the possibility of further hikes as they address persistent U.S. inflation.
Markets now see around a 70% probability of another rate increase in October. ANZ analysts said gold had fallen to about $4,130 an ounce as rising U.S. Treasury yields triggered a fresh selloff, while higher energy prices further increased expectations for a near-term Fed hike.
Fed Governor Lisa Cook said Monday that productivity gains from artificial intelligence may not be sufficient to offset near-term inflation pressures. She also said heavy investment in data centers was increasing competition for shared resources, including energy and construction labor.
ANZ said the near-term macroeconomic backdrop remains difficult for gold as higher yields and inflation risks weigh on the metal.
Markets will next focus on Wednesday's personal consumption expenditures inflation data, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, and Friday's nonfarm payrolls report for fresh clues on the path of interest rates.

title: Samsung, affiliates to invest $1 billion in AI infrastructure firm Helix
full_text:
U.S. stocks end down as OpenAI training halt weighs on AI trade, bonds extend rout
Investing.com -- Samsung Electronics (KS:005930) and five affiliates will invest a combined $1 billion in Helix Digital Infrastructure, an AI infrastructure company established by investment firm KKR, as the South Korean technology group expands its exposure beyond semiconductors and into data centers, power and connectivity.
Samsung Electronics will invest $500 million, with Samsung C&T, Samsung SDS, Samsung SDI, Samsung Life Insurance and Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance providing the remainder.
KKR, the Kuwait Investment Authority, Nvidia and U.S. power company Vistra are also founding investors in Helix.
Helix, launched in June, is designed to provide infrastructure across the AI value chain, including hyperscale data centers, power generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure and fiber-optic networks.
The company is led by former Amazon Web Services CEO Adam Selipsky and is building a management team drawn from the data-center and power industries.
The company described power availability as a major bottleneck for AI infrastructure and said Helix plans to secure capacity through direct investment and partnerships with energy developers, including Vistra.
The investment also brings together capabilities across Samsung’s businesses. Samsung Electronics supplies semiconductor solutions, while its Device eXperience division provides data-center cooling equipment through FläktGroup, which it acquired in 2025.
Samsung C&T works on data-center and power projects as an engineering, procurement and construction contractor, while Samsung SDS designs and operates data centers and has entered the GPU-as-a-service market.
Samsung SDI provides uninterruptible power supplies and battery backup systems for data centers and plans to explore additional business opportunities in the sector.
Samsung said the investment is intended to support global AI data-center deployment while allowing its affiliates to combine their hardware, engineering, cooling, power and data-center capabilities around Helix.

title: Shein shares hit record low as quarterly profit slumps 67%
full_text:
Investing.com-- Shein (HK:0625) shares fell to record lows on Tuesday after the fast-fashion retailer reported a steep decline in second-quarter profit, as higher oil prices and freight costs squeezed margins despite continued growth in orders.
Adjusted net income fell 66.6% to $228 million in the three months ended June 30, while net revenue rose just 0.9% to $11.08 billion, according to the company's interim report on Monday.
Hong Kong-listed shares of the company fell 12.7% to HK$30.8 by 03:55 GMT, reaching their lowest level on record. Shein shares debuted on Sept. 1.
Shein said its adjusted net income margin narrowed to 2.1% from 6.2% a year earlier, primarily because of a sharp rise in oil prices and freight rates amid Middle East geopolitical tensions.
The company said it chose to absorb those costs rather than pass them on to customers.
Fulfilment expenses rose 18.1% to $5.59 billion, accounting for 50.4% of revenue, compared with 43.1% a year earlier.
The results came despite a 7.6% increase in second-quarter orders, with active customers also rising. Shein said it expects tariff headwinds and logistics-cost volatility to persist in the second half, while remaining cautiously optimistic about adjusted net income.

title: Asian currencies mixed as dollar holds two-month high, RBA decision looms
full_text:

Investing.com -- Asian currencies were mixed on Tuesday, while the Japanese yen weakened toward recent lows as markets remained alert to intervention risks and assessed the Bank of Japan's policy path. The U.S. dollar held near a two-month high, while the Australian dollar awaited a widely expected interest rate hike.
Volatile oil prices and a sharp rise in Treasury yields supported the dollar, although gains were limited as investors waited for U.S. data later this week for clues on the Federal Reserve's rate path.
The U.S. dollar index was around 101.21, little changed, after reaching 101.27 earlier. It is on track for a 1.8% gain in September, which would be its strongest monthly performance since June. The USD/JPY pair was around 157.36.
Brent crude was around $106 a barrel as markets remained skeptical about renewed diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Iran conflict after President Donald Trump rejected Tehran's ceasefire proposal. The uncertainty has kept energy-supply risks elevated.
Dollar supported by yields, Fed hike bets
A selloff in U.S. Treasuries has pushed yields to fresh multi-year highs. The 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to its highest level since 2007, while the 30-year yield reached its highest since 2004.
The higher yields have supported the dollar, but the boost has been restrained as markets have become less reactive to oil-price swings and the global bond selloff has lifted yields elsewhere as well.
U.S. data due later this week could revive the rate debate. The PCE price index is due Wednesday, followed by nonfarm payrolls on Friday, with both expected to reinforce the case for additional Fed tightening.
Markets are now pricing more than a 70% chance of a Fed rate hike at the end of October, up from 57% a week ago.
Yen weakens as intervention warning returns
The yen weakened to around 157.36 per dollar, giving back much of Monday's earlier advance after Japan's top currency official Atsushi Mimura warned markets to heed a "very clear" message from Japan and the U.S. about excessive yen weakness.
The yen had strengthened as much as 0.4% to 156.51 on Monday, its strongest level since September 18, after Mimura's comments, but that move later faded.
Mimura's warning followed similar signals from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, who said U.S. President Donald Trump had also expressed concern about yen weakness.
Katayama and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had spoken by phone Friday and reaffirmed their view that the yen was undervalued while agreeing to deepen cooperation on currencies.
RBA decision puts Aussie in focus
The Australian dollar was around $0.70, little changed, ahead of the RBA's policy decision later Tuesday.
The central bank is widely expected to raise its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60%, its highest level since 2011.
DBS said the AUD/USD pair has found support around $0.70, but the Australian dollar has struggled to recover because much of the expected tightening is already priced in.
Renewed expectations for Fed hikes and elevated U.S. Treasury yields have also reduced Australia's rate advantage.
The New Zealand dollar was around $0.5675, while the USD/CNH pair fell 0.1% to 6.71 and USD/CNY also declined 0.1% to 6.71.
The South Korean won strengthened slightly, with USD/KRW around 1,357.54, while USD/INR traded flat. The USD/SGD rose 0.1% to 1.28.

NEW YORK, Sept 28 (Reuters) - CNN, MS NOW and Politico asked a federal judge late on Monday to issue a court order preserving their White House access while they fight US President Donald Trump’s move to ban them over coverage he dislikes.

title: Will a falling unemployment rate keep U.S. inflation above target?
full_text:
U.S. stocks end down as OpenAI training halt weighs on AI trade, bonds extend rout
Investing.com -- Over the past year, the U.S. labour force has contracted as unauthorised immigrants departed and the labour force participation rate declined. A recent note from BCA Research considers whether a falling unemployment rate will keep U.S. inflation above target.
The firm observes that the contraction in the U.S. labour force means the threshold for job growth to reduce the unemployment rate has been lowered. Investors are now asking if the labour market will tighten enough to keep inflation above the Fed’s target even if tariff and energy effects fade over the coming year.
Jonathan LaBerge of BCA Research notes that the Phillips Curve’s picture of the relationship between the unemployment rate and inflation is conflicting. He points out that from both 1999 to 2000 and from 2018 and 2019, there was a below 4% unemployment rate without high inflation. But there was much higher inflation along with low unemployment rates in the late 1960s and in the 2022 to 2024 period.
The Phillips Curve describes the relationship between inflation and unemployment over the short term, and is typically interpreted as showing that when demand is strong and unemployment low, there is inflationary pressure; weaker demand and higher unemployment, by contrast, reduce inflation.
The firm believes a below 4% unemployment rate might prove inflationary this time, given that the combination of low unemployment with low inflation seen in the 1990s was due to productivity gains. While AI might increase productivity at some point soon, no such gains are visible in the productivity data. Furthermore, from 2018-2019, inflation expectations were much lower, and that probably restrained wage growth.
“Our US Investment strategists see fears of a significant wage growth breakout as overdone. Entrenched misperceptions die hard, but the structural balance of power between workers and employers has shifted too far to permit a repeat of the 1970s,” LaBerge said.
He noted that the post-pandemic wage growth surge was due to a labour supply shortfall. At that time, the quit rate was at record levels, indicating there was poaching between firms, generous fiscal transfers had slowed down labour’s return to work, and employers attempting to fill openings had to bid up wages. These conditions no longer prevail.
The firm argues that the negligible cost of posting roles online has led to overstatement of current openings. It says the depressed hiring rate now shows that labour demand has subsided while the labour supply is squeezed due to immigration enforcement.
BCA Research believes that structural forces are in the favour of employers, while workers have less leverage against shareholder-focussed management as private-sector union membership has collapsed. The firm does not think that the forces responsible for causing a wage-price spiral are in action, and says worries about such a scenario are based on memories of exceptional labour policy actions that are very unlikely.
While a self-reinforcing loop of wages and prices driving each other higher is off the table, it remains a possibility that the Fed will deliver a hawkish surprise over the next 12 months, the firm added.

title: OpenAI apologies for Australian government website hack, pledges to rebuild trust
full_text:
U.S. stocks end down as OpenAI training halt weighs on AI trade, bonds extend rout
SYDNEY, Sept 29 (Reuters) - OpenAI apologised for the hacking of an Australian government website by a rogue AI agent, committing funding to improve cyber defences and to establish a local response taskforce as scrutiny mounts over the high-profile incident.
In a blog post on Tuesday titled "How we will do better for Australia", the ChatGPT maker acknowledged it mishandled its response and pledged to take accountability to "rebuild trust with the Australian people".
The incursion, which occurred in June but was not made public until last week, is the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.
The incident alarmed Australia, drawing public condemnation and a sharp rebuke from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who called it "unacceptable" and criticised the company’s delay in notifying the government.
"In June, during internal training and evaluation our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not authorised to," OpenAI said in the blog post. "We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future."
OpenAI said an experimental AI model breached the Services Australia Medicare Statistics Reporting Service, a data portal for the country’s universal healthcare system, during an internal training activity.
"An OpenAI model discovered a way to gain non-public access to the service, and ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, and wrote files," the company said.
But its review to date had not found any evidence of medical records being accessed from the portal, OpenAI said.
AI agent activity affecting three other Australian government agency websites also did not result in access to sensitive records, according to the company.
OpenAI said it would provide dedicated support for the affected agencies, finance the strengthening of cyber defences for government and industry through its $1 billion global fund and establish an Australian taskforce to develop recommendations "drawing on lessons from these incidents".
It also confirmed Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon would appear at an Australian Senate committee hearing on AI in Sydney on October 6.
The Australian government has announced a rapid review into the incident, examining potential notification and reporting obligations of AI companies and the adequacy of its laws in dealing with such breaches.
Separately, OpenAI has cancelled the release of its new AI model GPT-6.1 Astra after internal testing found the system did not meet the company’s safety standards.

1. Futures mixed
U.S. stock futures hovered around both sides of the flatline on Tuesday. By 03:28 ET (07:28 GMT), the Dow futures contract had dropped by 34 points, or 0.1%, S&P 500 futures were mostly unchanged, and Nasdaq 100 futures had risen by 20 points, or 0.1%.
The main averages on Wall Street retreated in the prior session, weighed down largely by the extended debt market selloff. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield hit a new 19-year high, while the longer-dated 30-year rate spiked to its most since 2004. Yields tend to move inversely to bond prices.
Underpinning the declines was President Donald Trump's decision to reject a fresh peace proposal from Iran that would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices rose, exacerbating worries that a prolonged energy shock could cause the Federal Reserve to raise rates multiple times this year. The Fed already lifted rates earlier this month -- its first since 2023.
2. Anthropic prospectus shows $2 trillion IPO ambition despite huge loss - Reuters
Anthropic is heading toward a public debut that could test investors’ appetite for the enormous spending and valuations underpinning the artificial intelligence boom, Reuters reported on Monday, citing the company’s IPO prospectus.
The AI startup expects a valuation of more than $2 trillion, more than double its estimated $965 billion value in May, the report said.
Revenue surged 12-fold in 2025 to nearly $4.6 billion, but Anthropic reported a $42 billion net loss, including a roughly $34 billion accounting charge tied to financing instruments that could convert into shares, Reuters reported.
The company spent $7.33 billion on computing and infrastructure last year, three times its 2024 outlay, while forecasting $518 billion in cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations over the coming year, the report stated.
3. OpenAI shelves new AI model release - WSJ
OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, its next-generation artificial intelligence model, after it failed internal safety controls, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.
The model– initially slated for an October release– was more capable than the startup’s previous models, the WSJ report said. The company will instead focus on improving the safety of its future models, which it expects to be even more capable.
OpenAI safety head Saachi Jain told the WSJ that Astra fell short of internal standards in alignment tests, and also displayed more deception than its predecessor.
The WSJ report comes amid growing debate over the risks posed by AI models. Reports over the weekend said OpenAI had paused training its newest AI models due to concerns over safety.
The company also disclosed that its models had targeted U.S. government websites in unexpected ways during training.
4. Oil prices rise
Oil prices rose on Tuesday, extending gains from the previous session, as a lack of progress in U.S.-Iran diplomacy kept concerns over Middle East supply disruptions in focus despite a recovery in crude exports from the region.
As of 03:15 ET, Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, had ticked up by 1.4% to $106.71 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 1.2% to $93.74 per barrel.
Brent futures had climbed near $109 per barrel in the previous session but pared gains to settle around $105 a barrel.
Qatari mediators were expected to hold separate talks with Iran's foreign minister and U.S. officials, with discussions focused on an amended seven-day proposal put forward by Iran last week, Reuters reported on Monday, citing sources. However, both sides remained pessimistic about reaching an agreement before the U.S. midterm elections in November.
The climb in oil prices comes even as media reports suggest that Saudi Arabia is once again exporting crude through an east-west pipeline that traverses the width of the country. Flows are said to be at about half of normal capacity in the line, which had been temporarily closed after it was attacked in drone strikes.
5. RBA rate hike
The Reserve Bank of Australia hiked interest rates to a near 15-year high on Tuesday, citing growing inflationary risks due to high energy prices and tight domestic capacity.
The RBA raised its cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.60%, its highest level since October 2011. The decision was unanimous, with all members of the RBA’s rate-setting board expressing concern over increasingly sticky inflation.
Tuesday’s hike was the RBA’s fourth such move in 2026, after it kicked off a tightening cycle earlier in the year.
The 25 bps hike was widely expected after a host of hawkish comments from RBA members, while recent Australian inflation data also read well above the central bank’s 2% to 3% annual target.

title: Julius Baer shares surge to 52-week high after FINMA closes enforcement case
full_text:

Investing.com -- Julius Baer Gruppe AG (SIX:BAER) shares surged to a 52-week high on Tuesday after Swiss regulator FINMA concluded a long-running enforcement procedure covering legacy risk-management and anti-money-laundering issues.
Julius Baer shares rose 7.18% to CHF76.74, significantly outperforming the broader Swiss market, with the SMI little changed in Tuesday trading. The stock traded close to its 52-week high of CHF77.26.
FINMA said Julius Baer committed serious breaches of supervisory requirements related to risk management and anti-money-laundering obligations. The investigation covered a major private-debt credit event and relationships with two Russian politically exposed persons.
The enforcement action centered partly on loans to a European group and its founder that eventually exceeded CHF1 billion. FINMA said the bank ignored warning signs and breached internal and regulatory risk limits, with an outstanding exposure of CHF586 million ultimately written down in full by the end of 2023. It also found deficiencies in the scrutiny of the source of assets connected to two high-risk Russian PEPs.
As part of the conclusion of the case, Julius Baer will be required to hold CHF250 million of additional CET1 capital, down from the previous CHF500 million requirement. The resulting de facto minimum CET1 ratio is 9.4%, while Julius Baer's reported CET1 ratio stood at 18.5% at the end of June.
The bank said the matters occurred before the appointment of its current management team and that it had already implemented remedial measures, including a revamped risk and compliance framework and changes to governance. It also said the wind-down of its private-debt business formed part of those measures.
Julius Baer said it remains focused on its 2026-2028 strategic cycle and its medium-term financial targets. The bank has also submitted a request to FINMA for approval to restart its share-buyback programme, pending final approval.

title: Blackstone to launch investment platform for Nordics warehouses

Investing.com -- Dutch engineering and consultancy group Arcadis (AS:ARDS) set targets for mid-single-digit organic revenue growth and long term profitability on Tuesday, while also announcing plans to streamline its portfolio and reduce overhead.
The company said it expects mid-single-digit organic net revenue growth over 2027-2029 and an operating EBITDA margin in the mid- to high-teens by 2029. It also targets a dividend payout ratio of 30%-40% of net income from operations and net debt of 1.5-2.5 times operating EBITDA.

The company also plans to reduce its overhead base by around 1,000 full-time employees in 2027, while continuing to hire in growth areas.
The company reaffirmed its 2026 guidance for low-single-digit organic net revenue growth and an operating EBITA margin of 11.7%-12.0%. On the new EBITDA basis, the company said that corresponds to a margin of 14.3%-14.6%.
Arcadis said its new strategy will focus investment on its Core and Accelerate businesses, while applying tighter margin discipline to areas it classifies as Optimize.
Core businesses, including transportation and energy and water, currently account for 53% of revenue, while Accelerate businesses, including industrial manufacturing and technology, account for 21%. Arcadis expects the combined share of Core and Accelerate businesses to rise from 74% of revenue to 85% by 2029.
Arcadis said AI and digital technologies will be embedded throughout the strategy, including through automation, standardized delivery and engineering workflows. More than 400 engineers across 17 countries are already using more than 700 AI-enabled workflows, according to the company.
The announcement comes shortly after WSP withdrew its proposed takeover of Arcadis, leaving the Dutch group to pursue its strategy independently. WSP had previously proposed €51.50 per Arcadis share.

title: Waldron long seen as next Goldman CEO. The question is when
full_text:
U.S. stocks end down as OpenAI training halt weighs on AI trade, bonds extend rout
By Saeed Azhar
NEW YORK, Sept 28 (Reuters) - John Waldron has long been seen as successor to Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon. The question was when the transition would happen.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday that the investment bank had discussed a plan for Solomon to step down as CEO and be replaced with Chief Operating Officer Waldron as soon as next year, citing people familiar with the matter.
"Of course the board regularly discusses succession, as we disclose in our filings, but there is no definitive timeline for succession at Goldman Sachs. Any assertions about timing are just speculation," Tony Fratto, Goldman’s global head of communications, said in a statement.
Solomon, 64, had been expected by senior staff to do 10 years in the CEO role, meaning he would likely stay in the position until 2028, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday. He was named CEO in October 2018.
CEO succession has become a key focus for investors across Wall Street. At JPMorgan Chase, attention has centered on when Jamie Dimon may step aside, while investors have also monitored leadership planning at Bank of America under Brian Moynihan, one of the longest-serving chiefs among major US banks.
Waldron, 57, has been expected to take over the reins from Solomon, sources familiar with the matter have said previously. His standing was further reinforced last year when he was appointed to the board and awarded a retention bonus.
Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Goldman Sachs’ succession has been ’unusually telegraphed’ and Waldron’s ascension has been expected since last year, when he was awarded the retention bonus.
It is unlikely that Waldron changes the bank’s strategy devised by Solomon.
"They have been driving Goldman’s priorities together," Mayo said.
OVERSEEING LEADERS OF BANK’S MAIN DIVISIONS
The Wall Street bank, which has been the top-ranked mergers and acquisitions adviser for two decades, has focused on growing its global banking and markets division, and wealth and asset management.
Goldman Sachs exceeded second-quarter profit expectations as dealmaking picked up and market volatility amid the US-Iran war boosted equities revenue to a record.
Solomon significantly scaled back the firm’s consumer banking by shedding assets after its foray into retail banking flopped.
Waldron, who has been president and chief operating officer since October 2018, oversees the leaders of the bank’s main divisions. He previously served as co-head of investment banking, a role he assumed in 2014 after joining Goldman in 2000.
Goldman shares were little changed in after-hours trading.
According to the WSJ report, discussions have involved Waldron taking over around the end of 2027 or in 2028.
Under the plan, Solomon would remain executive chairman for one to two years after stepping down from the CEO role, the report said.
The proposal would require approval from the bank’s board, and its timing could change, it said. The report added that approval could happen in the coming months.

title: US auto regulator closes airbag defect petition in about 807,000 Honda Odyssey cars

Sept 29 (Reuters) - A US auto regulator said on Tuesday it had closed a defect petition covering 806,963 Honda Odyssey vehicles in the United States over allegations of inadvertent airbag deployments while the vehicles were in motion.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said it had completed its review of a petition covering 2011 to 2017 Honda Odyssey vehicles and found insufficient evidence of a defect trend to warrant a formal probe.
The petition alleged that airbags could deploy without a sufficiently severe triggering event and that the airbag system was recording inaccurate diagnostic information.
The NHTSA said it reviewed consumer complaints and other reports alleging inadvertent deployments but did not identify a clear pattern or factor linking the incidents.
The agency also said it was not aware of any crashes or severe injuries resulting from the alleged deployments.
